https://www.dw.com/en/ceuta-spain-warns-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ISwS Nearly all of the people who rushed Ceuta's border have since left, but those who do stay are unlikely to be able to reach the European mainland unless they are formally granted permission to reside [FILE: August 6, 2026] Image: Violeta Santos Moura/REUTERS Advertisement Spain 's government on Friday threatened to impose reciprocal entry checks on travelers from Italy , unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni 's governemnt lifts the measures it has implemented by Sunday. Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week. The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes. Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy. Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did Spain say about possible checks on travelers from Italy? Spain called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population." Madrid had objected to the move on several grounds, saying it was based on "spurious arguments." It said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days . Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years. "If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said. Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15. Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zone amid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however. Italy first made the announcement as images and footage of the border breach were going viral online Image: Atlas/REUTERS What do we know about Italy's checks on travelers from Spain? Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground. Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure. "They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers." Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities. "I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough." EU defends border response after Ceuta crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Meloni and Sanchez: A clash of styles on migration At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration. Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe. Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market. Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare. "Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years." Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://telex.hu/after/2026/08/17/hayden.text: Menü Kereső Meghalt Hayden Panettiere After Nagy Nikoletta 36 éves korában meghalt Hayden Panettiere színésznő, írja az ABC News . Panettiere-t leginkább a Hősök című sorozatból ismerhette a magyar közönség, de játszott a Nashville-ben, a Hajrá csajokban és két Sikoly-filmben is. A lap a színésznő apjának közleményét idézte, aki azt írta: Panettiere tragikus hirtelenséggel halt meg. „Hihetetlenül ragyogó személyiség volt, igazi természeti erő, aki mérhetetlen szeretetet és örömöt adott mindenkinek, aki ismerte, és azoknak a millióknak is, akik a képernyőn látták” – áll a közleményben. A színésznő halálának körülményeiről egyelőre nem közöltek további részleteket. Panettiere ötéves korától, 1994-től szerepelt a képernyőn: pályafutását a One Life to Live, majd a Guiding Light című szappanoperákban kezdte. Később két Golden Globe-jelölést is kapott Juliette Barnes megformálásáért a Nashville című sorozatban. Panettiere korábban nyíltan beszélt arról, milyen nehézségekkel kellett megküzdenie gyerekszínészként, majd felnőttként is. Egy ideig alkohol- és drogproblémákkal küzdött. 2020-ban egy rehabilitációs intézményben kezelték. 2023-ban 28 éves öccse, Jansen váratlanul meghalt egy szívprobléma következtében. Idén májusban jelent meg This Is Me: A Reckoning című memoárja. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Friss az Afteren

https://english.radio.cz/prague-pride-20.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Prague Pride 2026 moves to Štvanice with ‘Times Are Changing’ theme Facebook Twitter Prague Pride 2026 moves to Štvanice with ‘Times Are Changing’ theme 4:05 ⨯ Prague Pride 2026 moves to Štvanice with ‘Times Are Changing’ theme https://english.radio.cz/prague-pride-2026-moves-stvanice-times-are-changing-theme-8893708#player=on Copy Share on social media Facebook X The annual Prague Pride festival gets under way on Monday with nearly 200 events across the Czech capital. This year's edition also brings a major change, with the festival moving from Letná Plain to its new main venue on Štvanice Island. I discussed the event with Prague Pride’s PR and media representative, Nikola Páleníčková. This year's Prague Pride theme is Times Are Changing. What inspired that theme and how will it be reflected in this year's programme? "This year's theme was inspired by the world we're living in right now more than any of our previous themes. “Queer people have generations of experience with change, adapting, resisting and building new ways of living together, and that experience feels valuable for society right now.” "We're living through a moment when the political map, legislation, language and social norms are all changing really fast. And that's true inside the queer community as well. "Change itself isn't bad or good, it just happens. What matters is how we respond to it and whether we can be there for each other. "Queer people have generations of experience with change, adapting, resisting and building new ways of living together. And that experience feels valuable for society right now, not just for us. So that's why we decided to go with this theme." Talking about change, the main Prague Pride venue is moving from Letná to Štvanice for the first time. Why did you decide to make that change and what can visitors expect? "It was mostly a production decision. Letná served us well for years, but it was getting harder and harder to work there from a production standpoint. It wasn't ideal for visitors either. There was a lot of heat, dust, sand and mud. "Štvanice is an island, so it's naturally more contained, which helps us a lot with both organisation and safety. I'd also say it has a much better summer atmosphere. It offers more shade, trees, grass and access to the river to cool off if needed. "That means the parade route changes too. Instead of crossing Čechův Bridge to get to Letná, we'll be crossing Hlávkův Bridge and ending on Štvanice Island." There are nearly 200 events taking place across Prague this year. What are some of the highlights you wouldn't want people to miss? "We definitely recommend visiting as many of them as possible. "Besides the opening on Monday, the closing ceremony and the big Pride Parade on Saturday, I'd probably pick the Greatest Queer Czech. It's a poll we're running with the Society for Queer Memory. They chose queer people who have always been part of Czech culture, and we'll announce the winner on Saturday. "The day before, at Betlémská kaple, we'll have 15 Years of Doodles. It's an evening of queer choirs from Philadelphia and Berlin, and it's a Prague premiere for both of them. "Then there's Stage Out, a brand new talent show in Pride Village, open to any queer performer, from complete beginners to seasoned acts. "So I encourage everyone to see those, and then explore the rest of the nearly 200 events." You already mentioned security. After the recent attack at Berlin Pride, have you stepped up security for this year's festival and the parade itself? "We know that a lot of people are shaken or grieving right now, and we are taking those events extremely seriously. "When it comes to the security of the festival itself, we're working closely with the Czech police, who'll be present throughout Prague Pride Village and during the whole parade. They'll probably increase the number of officers attending the parade as well. "There'll be security at every venue. Our team is specifically trained in de-escalation, and at the opening event in Prague Pride Village on Střelecký Island we'll be checking bags at the entrance. "And part of our response to the horrific Berlin attack will be holding a minute of silence at the beginning of the parade on Saturday."
